newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court sides with Florida in tobacco case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court sides with Florida in tobacco case.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court dealt a setback to a major tobacco company Monday by rejecting a challenge to a Florida law that allows the state to sue cigarette companies for the cost of smoking-related illnesses.

The high court rejected an appeal by Philip Morris Cos. Inc., the world's largest cigarette maker, and by Associated Industries of Florida Inc., one of the state's biggest business groups, urging the 1994 law be declared unconstitutional.
Their lawyers had argued in the appeal that the law violates the constitutional protections of due process by stripping from businesses their traditional defences against product liability.

But the justices, turning down the appeal without comment or dissent, let stand a Florida Supreme Court ruling that the state has the legal right to sue cigarette makers for Medicaid costs incurred by Florida from tobacco-related illnesses.
The Supreme Court action did not create a nationwide precedent, but cleared the way for Florida's case to proceed. A trial has been set for August.

The high court's action also may provide a boost to 21 similar state lawsuits brought against the tobacco industry. Suits also have been filed by a number of local governments, including New York City and the counties of Los Angeles and San Francisco.

Florida's civil lawsuit, filed in February 1995, seeks damages totalling nearly $1 billion. State officials estimated the Medicaid costs incurred by Florida to treat tobacco-related illnesses at more than $400 million a year.
The Florida Supreme Court in a 4-3 decision in June said the state could sue under the law.
The law stripped away the tobacco industry's traditional defence that smokers share the blame for their health problems because they made a personal choice to accept the risks.
It allowed the state to use statistical evidence to try to prove that tobacco was responsible for some of the illnesses.
In their challenge, Philip Morris and the state business group claimed the law was intended to "stack the deck" against tobacco firms and make sure the state won its lawsuit for monetary damages.

"It is as though the state has declared that in football league games, when the state university team's offence is on the field, the opponent's defence must withdraw to the sidelines," Philip Morris and the business group said.

They acknowledged that the tobacco industry had become "unpopular" with certain segments of public opinion and certain government officials, but said the high court "is particularly vigilant" to protect the rights of unpopular groups.
Florida urged the justices to deny the appeal, saying the law represented a sound attempt for force tobacco companies to pay some of the social costs stemming from their actions.
"Whether an individual smoker has assumed the risk of smoking is simply immaterial to the tobacco company's liability to the state," Attorney General Robert Butterworth said.
